senses.gloss:
kalaśa
(‘that which sounds [when filling with water]’)
------------------------------------------
The word ‘kalaśa’ is commonly used in two senses: a ceremonially established waterpot and the finial of a temple.
The waterpot कलश is used in many rituals. It is considered as a replica of the अमृतकलश, the celestial pot prepared by विश्वकर्म (the architect of the gods) at the time of churning the ocean, to hold the अमृत or nectar.
A कलश may be made of gold, silver, copper or even clay. The dimensions recommended are:
Maximum circumference: 101 cms. (40 inches)
Diameter of mouth: 16 cms. (6.4 inches)
Height: 32 cms. (12.8 inches)
It should be filled with water. Other things that may be put inside it are: precious stones, flowers, fruits and herbs.
The कलश is regarded as a composite divinity. ब्रह्मा, रुद्र, विष्णु and देवी are supposed to reside in its mouth, neck, bottom and middle part respectively.
It is sometimes described as containing in its belly, all the seven seas, all the seven islands as also all the प्लनेत्स् and the स्तर्स्. It is the replica of the whole universe.
Nine varieties of the kalaśas are also mentioned in some works. Eight are arranged in the eight directions and the ninth (called ‘indriyaghna,’ with five mouths) kept in the centre during certain rituals.
Establishment of a कलश is a must in the दुर्गापूजा.
The Kālikāpurāṇa (chapter 87) recommends that all gods should be worshipped in kalaśas only.
Coming to the कलश as the finial of the temple:
It is an important member of the superstructure over the sanctum of a temple. It may be made of copper or silver or gold. Inside it a ‘suvarṇapuruṣa’ (a golden person) is installed, with an elaborate ritual known as ‘hṛdayavarṇakavidhi’.

Kali
(‘he who ruins [one’s मिन्द् by sinful thoughts]’)
------------------------------------------
According to the पुराणस् कलि the presiding spirit of कलियुग or the Iron Age, is the personification of all that is bad and evil, the very antithesis of धर्म. He is the son of Krodha (anger) and हिṁसा (violence).
His wife is Durukti (harsh and bad speech), and son Bhaya (fear). Bhaya’s wife is मृत्यु (death) and son, Niraya (dark हेल्ल्).
Obviously all these are symbolical.
Kali’s images are very rare. When shown, he is depicted as dark in colour, hideous in appearance with the tongue lolling out.
Kali entered this world on the demise of Lord कृष्ण. Though vanquished by the king परीक्षित्, he was allowed to live in certain places, as mentioned below.
He is said to reside in गम्ब्लिन्ग्, liquor, wanton women and gold.

Kālikāpurāṇa
------------------------------------------
Purāṇas and उपपुराणस् have been responsible for preserving and spreading popular हिन्दुइस्म्. Among the eighteen उपपुराणस्, a Kālikāpurāṇa is also listed.
Two Kālikāpurāṇas have been dis-covered. While one is assigned to the period A. D. 1000, the other is dated as A. D. 1600.
The one available in print now has 7375 verses in 93 chapters. It seems to have been composed in Kāmarūpa (Assam) and has been considered an authoritative text quoted by later निबन्धस् like Kṛtyakalpataru and Dānasāgara.
The purāṇa deals with the exploits and worship of Kālī or Kālikā. She is primarily the योगनिद्रा or Vaiṣṇavīmāyā of विष्णु, reborn as सती first and later as पार्वती. The work contains a plethora of subjects connected with पिल्ग्रिमगे, worship of the various aspects of the देवी, various methods of पूजा, a lot of infor-mation regarding mantras, पुरश्चरण, yantras, spells and so on. Much of this information might have been drawn from works extant then, but not available now.

Kaliṅga
(‘[country established by] कलिङ्ग’)
------------------------------------------
The kingdoms of अङ्ग, Vaṅga and कलिङ्ग have been famous from very ancient times.
Kaliṅga was a prince who was the son of the sage दीर्घतमस्. The country conquered and ruled over by him came to be known as Kaliṅgadeśa. It is identified with the region between the rivers Mahānadī and गोदावरी, now in Orissa.
During the period of the rule of the Pāṇḍavas, one king, Citrāṇgada by name (a maternal uncle of दुर्योधन) was the ruler of this country. Rājapura was its capital.
Kaliṅga was famous for first rate elephants needed for the armed forces.

Kālarātri
(‘presiding goddess of the fierce night’)
------------------------------------------
Kālarātri is one of the several aspects of the Divine मोथेर् or a minor goddess presiding over the night that brings death and destruction.
She is dark in complexion, fierce in appearance and has a cruel laughter. She rides an ass.
If shown with four arms, she carries दण्ड (cudgel) and a लिङ्ग, the other two hands showing the varadamudrā (bestowal of boons).

Kālanirṇaya
------------------------------------------
Mādhava-विद्यारण्य (A. D. 1296-1386), the founder-saint of the विजय-nagara empire was a scholar of extra-ordinary brilliance. One of his well-known works is the Kālanirṇaya, a treatise on the definition of time and determination of suitable periods for religious occasions.
The work is in five prakaraṇas or chapters. The contents may be briefly stated as follows: scholastic disquisition on kāla or time; the year and its sub-divisions; intercalary months and religious acts permitted or forbidden during those months; about the tithis, pure and mixed and determination of the various nakṣatras for religious acts.
The work names numerous sages, पुराणस्, astronomical and astrological writers and their works.

kalpa
(‘era’)
------------------------------------------
Brahmā, the four faced creator, is the deity who creates our world. His lifespan is 100 divine years.
A कल्प is one day in his life. The च्रेअतिओन् lasts for this one day only. At the end of this day, there is प्रलय or dissolution, called ‘naimittika-प्रलय’. During ब्रह्मा’s night there will be no च्रेअतिओन्.
Each कल्प is divided into 14 manvantaras and one मनु rules over each of them.
We are now passing through the first कल्प (called ‘Śvetavarāhakalpa’) of the 51st year of ब्रह्मा. Of the 14 manvantaras, the 7th is now in progress, ruled over by वैवस्वत मनु.
A कल्प is also divided into 1000 चतुर्युगस् or sets of four युगस्. One मनु rules over 1000/14 or 71.42 catur-युगस्. The present मनु is now in the कलियुग of the 28th caturyuga.
In terms of Human years, one कल्प is 4.32 billion years.
See also YUGAS.

kalpanāgaurava
(‘excessive imagination’)
------------------------------------------
This is one of the eleven varieties of तर्क or लोगिच्.
To say that all pots in this world are one and the same since they are made of the same material (clay) and have the same quality of ‘potness’—is the example given to substantiate the term.

Kālīghāṭ Temple
------------------------------------------
The city of Calcutta (now Kolkata) was originally a small place called Kālīkāta (land belonging to Kālī), containing an ancient shrine of मोथेर् Kālī.
This temple, now known as the कालीघाट् तेम्प्ले, is a landmark in the city, visited by thousands of people everyday.
There are several stories as to how this original shrine situated in a jungle, was discovered.
A ब्राह्मण bathing in the river भागीरथी (Gaṅgā) saw a ray of light emerging out of water in a particular spot. Diving there, he discovered a piece of stone carved like a human toe. Later in the night he dreamed that, that was the toe of the goddess सती दाक्षायणी (Pārvatī).
According to the tradition regarding the च्रेअतिओन् of शक्तिपीठस् (places sacred to शक्ति or the Divine मोथेर् पार्वती) this place is considered the second one where the toe of सती दाक्षायणी fell. (See under TANTRAS for details.)
The ब्राह्मण also discovered a शिवलिङ्ग in the nearby area. He established the stone image of the toe there and started worshipping them.
(This शिवलिङ्ग is called Nakuleśvara.)
It is round these icons that gradually a big temple developed due to the efforts of devotees.
A few other stories connected with this temple may be summarised as follows:
Santosh Roy Choudhury of the famous Sabarṇa Roy Choudhury family discovered this image in a jungle following the sound of a conch which he accidentally heard one day while passing by. It was he who first started to build a temple for it and to worship it. It was his son Ram Lal and nephew Rajiv who completed the construction of the temple in A. D. 1809.
Keshav Roy Choudhury, another scion of the Sabarṇa family, discovered the image through a dream revelation. He brought it out and built a small temple for it. The present temple was built later by Rajiv Lochan Roy.
Some Kāpālikas (See under ŚAIVISM.) discovered the image in a forest and fixed it there itself.
Cauraṅgi Giri, a saṁnyāsin of the Daśanāmī Order, discovered the image and had it consecrated in a temple.
There is a reference to one भुवनेश्वर Brahmacāri who was the priest of this temple in A. D. 1550, thereby confirming the existence of the temple even by that time. He had allowed the fixing of Śālagrāmas in the temple which can be seen even now.
The कालीघाट् तेम्प्ले is situated on the bank of the river भागीरथी (or गङ्गा).
The image of मोथेर् Kālī is made of Koṣṭi stone which is black in colour. The hands of मोथेर् Kālī are adorned with golden bangles and bracelets. Her nose-ring also is of gold. She holds a silver sword in one hand and a severed head in the other. She wears a garland of human heads made of gold and silver. Her teeth and tongue too are covered with gold.
She wears a golden crown above which there is a golden umbrella. The whole body is covered with cloths and numerous flower garlands adorn her neck. Lord शिव is lying prostrate at her feet. His image is also covered with silver.
The Nakuleśvar शिव temple (built in A. D. 1805) is in front of the Kālī temple.
The nāṭmandir (assembly hall or pavilion) has an image of Lord कृष्ण as वासुदेव. It is offered vegetarian ड़ोओद्.
Sacrifice of goats to मोथेर् Kālī is very common.
Many poor people are fed everyday.
See also KĀLĪ.

Kalki
------------------------------------------
Lord विष्णु whose duty it is, to take care of the world after its च्रेअतिओन्, incarnates himself whenever धर्म (righteousness) declines and अधर्म (unrighteousness) gets the upper hand, to restore the balance.
Out of the ten avatāras or such incar-nations—generally known as ‘Daśāvatāras’—Kalki is the last and is yet to come. He is said to appear at the end of the कलियुग as the son of Viṣṇuśarma and Sumati at the city of Śambalāpura. He will finish his एदुचतिओन् under परशुराम, please परमेश्वर by his तपस्, obtain a divine sword and a steed from him, and then kill कलि in a combat, thus freeing the world from his unrighteous rule.
In this इन्चर्नतिओन्, पद्मावती, the princess of Siṁhala will be his queen.
See also AVATĀRA.

Kalpataru
(‘wish-yielding tree’)
------------------------------------------
In the Hindu mythological works, a कल्पतरु (also called Kalpadruma or Kalpavṛkṣa) is often mentioned as a divine tree situated in हेअवेन्, in the garden of इन्द्र. It is said to have emerged out of the क्षीरसमुद्र (ocean of milk) at the time of churning it by the देवस् (gods) and the दानवस् (demons). Its special quality is that it fulfils the desires of persons sitting under it.
According to another version, it is one of the five divine trees found in हेअवेन्, the other four being Mandāra, पारिजात, Santāna and Haricandana.
Kalpataru is also the name of a scholarly commentary by Amalānanda (13th century A. D.) on the Bhāmatī of वाचस्पति (A. D. 840) which itself is a detailed gloss on the Brahmasūtrabhāṣya of शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820).

kalivarjya
(‘what is prohibited in the age of कलि’)
------------------------------------------
Hinduism has two important sets of teachings: The Śruti and the स्मृति. The Śruti or the वेदस् (including the उपनिषद्स्) concern themselves mainly with the ultimate truths of life and the ultimate goal of life as also the means of achieving it.
The smṛtis, on the other hand, are handbooks of social values and conduct, regulating the current-day societies. As changes take place in a society due to external and internal factors, the smṛtis also have revised their rules and regulations to be in tune with the changes. The principle of कलिवर्ज्य is a typical example of this healthy attitude and flexibility.
The principle of Kalivarjya—what was once permitted in the earlier ages, but now to be given up or prohibited in this age of Kali—seems to have made its appearance around A. D. 1000, mostly in the पुराणस्.
Scholars have listed 55 items as कलिवर्ज्य. Some of these are: giving a larger share of property to the first or eldest son; नियोग (levirate); remarriage of widows; intercaste marriages; read-mission of a ब्राह्मण into the fold even after sea voyage; sattra sacrifices; killing of a cow in the sacrifice called Gosava; वानप्रस्थ stage; the sale of the सोम creeper by a ब्राह्मण; allowing a ब्राह्मण to eat the ड़ोओद् of persons of lower varṇas which had been permitted earlier; पिल्ग्रिमगे to very distant holy places; begging of ड़ोओद् by a saṁnyāsin from all varṇas; engaging a śūdra for cooking in the होउसे of a ब्राह्मण; resorting to सṁन्यास; observance of अग्निहोत्र; performance of अश्वमेध and राजसूय sacrifices; perpetual studenthood (naiṣṭhika ब्रह्मचर्य); अनिमल् सच्रिड़िचेस्; intoxicating drinks.
Though it is difficult to say on what basis these rules or recommendations were made, except a few of them like the first two items, the rest do not seem to be very relevant. What is really needed is the educational, economic and cultural upliftment of the Hindu society based on the age-old spiritual values as depicted in the उपनिषद्स् and the Bhagavadgītā.

Kālabhairava
------------------------------------------
Kālabhairava (an aspect of शिव) is the guardian deity of काशी (Vārāṇasī). The story goes that he nipped the fifth head of ब्रह्मा, the creator, because of his arrogant behaviour. This head or skull, stuck to शिव’s hand and as a penance he had to wander about for 12 years as a mendicant. When he took bath at a particular pool in वाराणसी, the skull fell off. Since then, the pool has become known as ‘Kapālamocanatīrtha’.
The word ‘Kālabhairava’ means one who is terrific (= भैरव) even to यम, the god of death (= kāla).
Kālabhairava is also known as ‘Brahmaśiraścchetṛmūrti’.
In iconographical works he is described as white in complexion with three eyes and the hair dressed as a crown atop the head (jaṭāmukuṭa). His ear-ornaments are patra or tāṭaṅka (leaf) and makarakuṇḍala (mythical crocodile). In his four hands he carries परशु (battle-axe), वज्र (thunderbolt), śūla (spear) or त्रिशूल (trident) and Brahmakaroṭikā (Brahmā’s skull).
As per other descriptions he is shown with sword, trident, kettle-drum (ḍamaru) and skull. He wears a garland of beads made of bones.
He is accompanied by a dog, just to indicate that he is the guardian deity (Kṣetrapāla) of the sacred sites.

kalpanālāghava
(‘simple imagination’)
------------------------------------------
Samavāya (inherence) has been accepted as one of the seven padārthas or categories by the Vaiśeṣika philosophy. The connection that exists between the parts and the whole, a moving object and the movement itself, a quality and the object that possesses it—these are examples of समवाय.
Is समवाय only one or many? Though it may exist in many forms, it is actually one only. This kind of argument is कल्पनालाघव. It is one of the eleven forms of तर्क.

Kalisantaraṇa Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
The Kalisantaraṇa Upaniṣad is a short work in prose, classed among the minor उपनिषद्स् of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda and propagating वैष्णविस्म्.
The sage नारद, observing that the द्वापरयुग had come to an end and that the कलियुग had just begun, approached ब्रह्मा (the creator) and asked how he could overcome the evil effects of कलि (the Iron Age and its sinful effects). ब्रह्मा replied that this could be done by the repetition of the name of नारायण, the primeval person (Ādi-पुरुष). On being requested to reveal it, ब्रह्मा replied that the मन्त्र was:
hare राम hare rāma
rāma राम hare hare ।
hare कृष्ण hare kṛṣṇa
kṛṣṇa कृष्ण hare hare ॥
This मन्त्र of sixteen parts is capable of destroying the sixteen covers (vide Praśna Upaniṣad 6.4) binding the सोउल्. When that happens, then the सोउल् will shine like the sun, after the clouds that were covering it, are driven away by a powerful wind.
There are no hard and fast rules regarding the repetition of this मन्त्र. Whether one is clean or unclean, by repeating it, one can get लिबेरतिओन् in the form of attaining God’s world, living near him, becoming like him in form or even getting dissolved in him.
By doing जप of this मन्त्र 35 millions of times, a person becomes freed from even the most heinous sins like ब्रह्महत्या or stealing gold and so on.
See also UPANIṢADS.

kālakṣepa
------------------------------------------
It is also known as kathākālakṣepa.
See HARIKATHĀ.

Kalpasūtras
(‘treatises dealing with practical aspects’)
------------------------------------------
The कल्प or the कल्पसूत्रस् is one of the six वेदाङ्गस् or subsidiary treatises that help in the conducting of वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्.
‘Kalpa’ means prayoga or the practical methods.
The कल्पसूत्रस् belong to a period later than that of the major उपनिषद्स्.
The work has four sub-branches. They are: श्रौतसूत्रस्, गृह्यसूत्रस्, धर्मसूत्रस् and शुल्बसूत्रस्.
The श्रौतसूत्रस् deal with वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्. The गृह्यसूत्रस् deal with domestic rites and rituals. The धर्म-sūtras deal with the varṇāśrama dharmas. The शुल्बसूत्रस् contain detailed information about the construction of the altars for वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्.
See under each title for more details.

kalā
(‘that which increases’)
------------------------------------------
Sanskrit is a marvellous language. This word ‘kalā’ is one that has several meanings. Any interpretation depends on the context in which it is used.
Normally, it is used in the sense of a ‘part’ (generally 1/16) of anything.
When it refers to an art or science, 64 of them are listed. Some of them are: gītam (music), nṛtyam (dancing), puṣpā-staraṇam (decoration with flowers), aindrajāla (magic), prahelikā (giving riddles for solving), takṣakarma (carpentry), vāstuvidyā (architecture), निमित्त-ज्ञान (futurology with the help of omens), dhātuvāda (metallurgy) and so on.
In आयुर्वेद (health-science) it refers to the seven parts of a human body.
The उपनिषद्स् sometimes refer to 16 kalās or parts like प्राण (life force), indriya (sense organ), तपस् (austerity) and so on as associated with a living being and responsible for his bondage (Praśna Upaniṣad 6).

Kālidāsa
(‘servant of Kālī’)
------------------------------------------
If कालिदास has been universally acclaimed as the brightest star among the great authors of Sanskrit literature, and one of the greatest poets and dramatists of the world, he richly deserves it.
Though he is so well-known, his date has not been fixed with any certainty. It varies from the 2nd century B. C. up to the 4th century A. D. However, based on an embossed metallic piece discovered at Bhiṭa (20 kms. or 12 miles from Allahabad in Uttar Pradesh) during archaeological excavations, some modern scholars have tried to fix his date as 2nd century B. C.
Many stories are current in the popular literatures of India regarding his life. According to most of these, he was a dunce who became a highly evolved scholar and poet overnight by his devotion to मोथेर् Kālī.
According to other versions, he was a ब्राह्मण of good Śaiva parentage, highly educated and cultured. He was one of the nine jewels in the court of the king विक्रमादित्य (whose identity has not been established conclusively).
Kālidāsa’s works are:
DRAMAS: Abhijñāna-śākuntala;Vikramorvaśīya; Mālavikāgnimitra.
POETICAL WORKS: (called ‘Mahākāvyas’)Raghuvaṁśa; Kumārasambhava; Meghadūta; Ṛtusaṁhāra.
Abhijñānaśākuntala depicts the story of the king दुष्यन्त and शकुन्तला, the adopted daughter of the sage कण्व.
The story of the king Vikrama (also known as Purūrava) and the celestial nymph ऊर्वशी is the main theme of the drama Vikramorvaśīya. So also, the love story of Mālavikā, the princess of Vidarbha and Agnimitra, the king of Vidiśā has been depicted in the drama Mālavikāgnimitra.
The Raghuvaṁśa is a long poetical work classed among the Mahākāvyas. It is in 19 sargas or cantos. It deals with the stories of 23 kings of the race of the रघु, though, for obvious reasons, the story of राम gets the pride of place.
Though the Kumārasambhava is in eighteen cantos, कालिदास, perhaps, wrote only the first seven, the other eleven being the handiwork of an inferior author. It describes the मर्रिअगे of शिव and पार्वती and the birth of कुमार (also known as सुब्रह्मण्य or कार्त्तिकेय) who later killed the demon Tāraka.
The Meghadūta is a small work that graphically describes the pangs of separation of a यक्ष from his beloved wife.
The Ṛtusaṁhāra gives a graphic description of the ṛtus or seasons. कालिदास was, without doubt, the super-master of Indian poetic style. His upamās or allegories have been considered as the very best and models for other writers.

Kālayavana
------------------------------------------
The Yādavas once offended their priest, the sage गर्ग. गर्ग prayed to शिव to give him a son who could destroy the Yādavas. कालयवन was that son born to a celestial nymph from गर्ग.
Kālayavana was a very powerful warrior and demoniacal by nature. He harassed the Yādavas many times and had even attacked द्वारका, their capital.
Once, when he attacked द्वारका, कृष्ण tactfully drew him away, ran into a dark mountain cave where the great king मुचुकुन्द was sleeping and hid himself. कालयवन, entered the cave and kicked the king thinking that he was कृष्ण. When the king opened his eyes and saw कालयवन, the latter was immediately reduced to ashes, as a result of the boon he had received from the gods whom he had helped in their fight against the demons.

Kālindī
(‘that which originates from the hill Kalinda’)
------------------------------------------
The river यमुना is well-known in the Vaiṣṇava पुराणस् as कालिन्दी. (See YAMUNĀ for details.)
One of the eight queens of Śrī कृष्ण was कालिन्दी, daughter of सूर्य and sister of यमुना. She married him after performing severe austerities, knowing that he was विष्णु himself. While on a hunting mission, कृष्ण found her in a forest and married her after knowing her intentions. She bore him ten valiant sons.
One of the ponds of the यमुना river was also known as कालिन्दी. A sage Saubhari had once cursed गरुड not to come to this pond to eat up the snakes there. Consequently many snakes including the terrible Kāliyanāga had made it their habitation.

Kālāgnirudra
------------------------------------------
This is one of the terrific forms of रुद्र or शिव, denoting the destructive fire or ‘fire of death’ (= kālāgni). He is shown with four arms holding खड्ग (sword), खेटक (shield), धनुस् (bow) and बाण (arrow). He wears garments of red colour.
Sometimes he is shown among the Bhairavas (generally 64 in number). In this case he carries kuṇḍa (water pot), खेटक (shield), parigha (iron club) and bhiṇḍipāla (hand javelin).
In the works on शैवसिद्धान्त, kālāgni represents one of the regions of the earth-element.

Kālaḍī
------------------------------------------
Almost all the traditional biographies of शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820) declare that he was born at कालडी (or Kālaṭī), a small town situated on the bank of the river Pūrṇā (or Periyār). It is the same as the modern town कालडी (or Kalady) in the Ernakulam district of Kerala State. It is about 13 kms. (8 miles) from Alwaye, 45 kms. (28 miles) from Kochi (Cochin) and 55 kms. (34 miles) from the city of Trichur.
Kālaḍī TempleA chieftain, Rājaśekhara by name, is said to have founded the original village of कालडी. He had a dream in which he saw a self-manifested शिवलिङ्ग at this place. After discovering it, he built a temple and a colony for the ब्राह्मणस् and others who took care of it.
Vidyādhirāja was one of these first settlers, Śivaguru, the ड़थेर् of शङ्कर was his son.
The शारदा मठ of Śṛṅgerī has a branch here, at the very place where शङ्कर’s original होउसे was situated. There are two temples here, one of goddess Śāradāmbā and the other of शङ्कर as Dakṣiṇāmūrti
A black pole to the left of the main entrance is believed to mark the exact place where शङ्कर was born.
The other places of interest are: a memorial which marks the place where Āryāmbā (Śaṅkara’s मोथेर्) was cremated; the Crocodile Ghāṭ, the bathing place in the Pūrṇā river where the boy शङ्कर is said to have been attacked by a crocodile and the श्रीकृष्ण temple, कृष्ण being family deity of शङ्कर.
The erstwhile Śaṅkarācārya of the Kāñcī Kāmakoṭi पीठ (Candraśekha-rendra Sarasvati [ A. D. 1894-1994]) has built a monument called ‘Ādi शङ्कर Kīrtistambha मण्डप’ in कालडी. It is 45 metres (147 ft.) high and has nine storeys. There are illustrations in the form of relief paintings depicting the story of शङ्कर.
The Śṛṅgerī शारदा मठ is running a Sanskrit University here.
See also ŚAṄKARA.

Kaliyuga
(‘the age of कलि’)
------------------------------------------
The concept of time as given in the पुराणस्, to say the least, is मिन्द्-boggling. One year of the human beings is one day of the celestials. Twelve-thousand such celestial years form one Caturyuga or the period of four युगस् of Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara and कलि.
The duration of the कलियुग in terms of human years in 4,32,000 years. कलियुग is supposed to have started on the 18th February 3102 B. C. Of course, there are other dates given by scholars and there is no unanimity among them. Some reckon it from the day of the beginning of the महाभारत war and others from the day of the ascension of Śrī कृष्ण.
At present, the 5101st year of the कलियुग has begun (from the 15th April 2000).
The age of कलि or कलियुग has been described as an age of evil and sin.
The itihāsas and the पुराणस् give a highly graphic but pessimistic account of the कलियुग.
Here is a sample: All men will be liars. ब्राह्मणस् will give up the sacred way of life prescribed for them. शूद्रस् will acquire wealth and will be intent on doing जप. Many mleccha kings will rule over the earth. They will be sinful and oppressive. People will be short-lived. They will be weak, both physically and mentally. Kṣattriyas and vaiśyas will oppress the society. Ferocious animals will increase in number. Women will be of loose character. False अस्चेतिच्स् will cheat the gullible persons.
Though a general decline of moral values seems to be what is intended by these descriptions, they are highly exaggerated.
See also YUGAS.

Kalmāṣapāda
(‘one with black feet’)
------------------------------------------
Some of the stories in the itihāsas and the पुराणस् are not only interesting but also instructive. The story of कल्माषपाद is, perhaps, one such.
The king Saudāsa of the इक्ष्वाकु dynasty was once tricked by a demon into serving his गुरु वसिष्ठ with human flesh. He was consequently cursed by the angered sage to become a cannibal-demon. Saudāsa, who was now called Kalmāṣa-pāda (since his feet were black) ate up all the sons of वसिष्ठ himself. However, after the twelve year period of the curse was over, वसिष्ठ was kind enough to bless him with a good son to succeed him.
